From the late 700s to the 900s, scholars in Baghdad translated much of Greek science and philosophy into Arabic, paid by the Abbasid caliphs and their courtiers. The chart's date, 830, is around when the caliph al-Ma'mun gave the work its biggest push; tradition ties it to his library, the House of Wisdom.

The translators, many of them Syriac-speaking Christians such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq, rendered Aristotle, the medicine of Galen, the geometry of Euclid and the astronomy of Ptolemy, often by way of older Syriac versions. Persian and Indian works came too, among them the Indian numerals.

The translations fed new work: al-Khwarizmi on algebra, al-Kindi on philosophy, and later Avicenna and Ibn al-Haytham. Paper, newly made in the Islamic world, kept copying cheap. From the 1100s many of these Arabic texts were put into Latin in Spain and Sicily, carrying Greek learning back to western Europe with Arabic additions.
